conversations.segment_role: Establish initial name preferences and introduce control target

dialogue.content: Hey, I want to make sure I keep track of how certain people in my life prefer to be addressed. My college friend Marcus told me he strictly goes by "Marcus" — full name, no nicknames. He was really clear about it when we reconnected back in January. He said he'd had too many people shortening it to Marc or Mark and it drives him up the wall. Can you help me keep a running note of these preferences?

Of course! I'd be happy to help you track your contacts' preferred names and forms of address. I've noted the first one: your college friend Marcus prefers to be called by his full name, "Marcus," and specifically dislikes shortened versions like Marc or Mark. He made this clear when you reconnected in January. If you have more people to add, just let me know and I'll keep everything organized so you can reference it before sending emails or making introductions. It's a thoughtful thing to track — getting someone's name right really matters.

Absolutely, it matters a lot to me. The next one is my roommate Chen Wei — he prefers people use his full name "Chen Wei" rather than just "Wei." He told me this on May 2nd when we caught up over the phone. Apparently a lot of people at his new job default to calling him Wei and it really bothers him. I want to make sure I always introduce him properly as Chen Wei.

Got it — your roommate Chen Wei prefers to be addressed by his full name, "Chen Wei," not just "Wei." He shared this on May 2nd during a phone call, and it's especially important because coworkers at his new job have been defaulting to just his second name, which frustrates him. I'll make sure this is noted alongside Marcus's preference. So far we have: Marcus wants his full name used, no nicknames; Chen Wei wants both parts of his name used, not just Wei. Let me know if there are others you'd like to add to the list.

Okay, here's an important update. Marcus actually changed his mind — he told me around mid-March that he now goes by "Marc" in all professional settings. He started using it at his consulting firm after he got promoted in February. He said the shorter version feels more authoritative and polished in meetings. So please update that — it's Marc now, not Marcus, especially for work-related stuff.

Updated! As of mid-March, your college friend Marcus now prefers to go by "Marc" in professional settings. He made the switch after getting promoted at his consulting firm in February, feeling that the shorter name sounds more authoritative and polished. I've revised the note accordingly: Marc (formerly insisted on Marcus) for professional contexts. Chen Wei's preference remains the same — full name "Chen Wei," not just Wei. I'll keep both of these current. If Marcus's preference shifts again or if you want to distinguish between casual and professional contexts, just let me know.

That's perfect. I also want to mention that my coworker David doesn't really care whether people call him Dave or David — he told me that in April. So that one's low stakes, but I figured I'd note it anyway just for completeness. It's nice when someone is easygoing about their name, even if it's less urgent to track.

Noted — your coworker David is fine with either "Dave" or "David" and has no strong preference either way, as he mentioned in April. It's definitely lower stakes than the others, but it's good to have for completeness. Here's your current list: Marc (college friend) — prefers "Marc" professionally since mid-March; Chen Wei (roommate) — always use full name "Chen Wei," not just Wei; David (coworker) — no preference between Dave and David. Let me know whenever you need to reference or update any of these, and I'll keep everything accurate for you.
